subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How long is the Paper 1: Reading examination for Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500)?
questions.explain: Paper 1: Reading is a 2-hour written examination.

questions.q: What is the total number of marks available for Paper 1: Reading?
questions.explain: Paper 1: Reading carries a total of 80 marks.

questions.q: Across the whole qualification, reading skills carry what overall weighting?
questions.explain: Reading and writing are each weighted at 50% of the qualification.

questions.q: How many reading passages are set on the Paper 1 question paper?
questions.explain: Paper 1 presents three texts (Text A, Text B and Text C) for candidates to read.

questions.q: Which reading assessment objective involves demonstrating understanding of explicit meanings?
options: Selecting and using information for a specific purpose
questions.explain: One reading objective is to demonstrate understanding of the text's explicit, directly stated meanings.

questions.q: Which reading assessment objective focuses on how writers achieve effects and influence readers?
options: Understanding how writers achieve effects and influence readers
questions.explain: A key reading objective is to demonstrate understanding of how writers achieve effects and influence readers.

questions.q: In the 'writer's effects' question, candidates are mainly required to:
options: select powerful or unusual words and phrases and explain their effects
correct the grammatical errors in the passage
translate the passage into formal English
count the number of adjectives the writer uses
questions.explain: The writer's effects task rewards selecting striking language and explaining the effect it creates for the reader.

questions.q: When writing the summary response, candidates are advised to use:
options: direct quotations copied straight from the text
their own words as far as possible
questions.explain: A good summary re-expresses the relevant points concisely in the candidate's own words.

questions.q: A question asking what a text 'suggests' about a character is mainly testing the ability to:
options: evaluate the writer's use of punctuation
questions.explain: Words such as 'suggests' signal that the reader must infer implicit meaning rather than quote a stated fact.

questions.q: The 'connotations' of a word refer to:
options: the ideas and associations it suggests beyond its literal meaning
the number of syllables it contains
questions.explain: Connotations are the associations and feelings a word carries beyond its literal (denotative) meaning.

questions.q: Why are candidates advised to quote short, precise words rather than long sentences in the writer's effects answer?
options: to save time in the examination
so the analysis can focus closely on the effect of specific word choices
to fill more space on the page
questions.explain: Short, precise quotations let the candidate zoom in on the effect of individual, carefully chosen words.

options: include the candidate's personal opinions and examples
concisely select and reorganise the relevant points from the text
focus mainly on analysing the writer's language
questions.explain: Summary rewards selecting the relevant points and re-organising them concisely, not analysis or personal comment.

questions.q: The objective 'analyse, evaluate and develop facts, ideas and opinions' requires candidates to:
options: support their analysis with appropriate reference to the text
list the events only in chronological order
questions.explain: This objective asks candidates to analyse and develop ideas using appropriate support drawn from the text.

questions.q: Analysing the 'structure' of a text involves considering:
options: how ideas are organised and ordered across the text
questions.explain: Structural analysis considers how a writer organises and sequences ideas to shape meaning and effect.

questions.q: Being able to distinguish between fact and opinion in a passage is an example of:
options: reading and understanding the text critically
questions.explain: Separating fact from opinion is part of reading and understanding a text critically and closely.

questions.q: The reading objective about selecting and using information for a specific purpose is most directly tested by:
questions.explain: The summary task directly assesses selecting and using relevant information for a specific purpose.

questions.q: A writer describes a crowded street as 'a river of people flooding the pavements.' The best comment on this metaphor is that it:
options: tells the reader exactly how many people there were
suggests the large, unstoppable and continuous movement of the crowd
shows the street was next to an actual river
criticises the people for arriving late
questions.explain: The 'river'/'flooding' imagery conveys a vast, overwhelming, continuous flow of people.

questions.q: A text reads: 'She checked the clock for the third time and tapped her foot.' A reader can best infer that the character is:
questions.explain: Repeatedly checking the clock and tapping her foot implies impatience or anxiety.

questions.q: For a writer's effects answer, which quoted phrase offers the richest opportunity for analysis?
options: 'the menacing shadow clawed across the wall'
questions.explain: The vivid personification and connotations of 'menacing' and 'clawed' give the most to analyse in terms of effect.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500) syllabus; Paper 1: Reading
